questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a seat share above a vote share indicates about representation.
questions.stem: In my spring log I note that the Ashcombe branch candidates took 34% of the branch vote but won 47% of the seats on the association committee.

options.text: Seat share exceeded vote share, so the electoral system gave that party seats beyond its votes
The result was disproportional because the branch counts ballots in a way I cannot verify
options.misconception: blames the counting method without any evidence of irregularity

options.text: The result was proportional because the winning party won more seats than it lost
options.misconception: measures proportionality by seat losses rather than vote shares

options.text: The result was impossible because no party can win more seats than it polled
options.misconception: assumes a mathematical ceiling that does not exist

questions.explanation: Proportionality compares a party's share of seats with its share of votes. Here 47% of seats against 34% of votes means representation ran ahead of support, which is what the term describes.
questions.hint: Compare the two percentage shares side by side.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Assess the effect of an observation excluded from a published count.
questions.stem: My logbook for the winter records that a ballot box from the hill apiary reached the count a week after the results were published, and it contained four votes for the candidate who had lost by three.

options.text: The published result stands, because a count cannot be reopened once it is announced
options.misconception: assumes finality that the count's own terms do not guarantee

options.text: The result may be misstated, because a decisive observation was excluded from the count
The result stands, because the box missed the deadline for returning ballot papers
options.misconception: invents a returning deadline the logbook never states

options.text: The whole election must be rerun, because one late box invalidates every count
options.misconception: prescribes a total rerun rather than a correction of the count

questions.explanation: An observation that would have changed the outcome was excluded, so the published figure rests on an incomplete count. Whether it must now be included is a question of the rules, not of lateness alone.
questions.hint: Ask whether the published count covered every ballot.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a survey lead while accounting for undecided voters.
questions.stem: During the branch meeting I noted in my logbook that the spring survey put the amber party at 41%, the blue at 36%, and 23% undecided, three months before the vote.

options.text: The amber party is certain to win, because a five point lead is decisive on any measure
options.misconception: treats a survey lead as a settled outcome rather than a snapshot

options.text: The amber party is certain to lose, because most voters said they would not back them
options.misconception: reads a below-majority preference as a likely defeat for the party

options.text: The lead is real but fragile, because undecided voters and late swings decide margins
The survey is worthless, because no survey can indicate an election result at all
options.misconception: dismisses all polling rather than weighing what it can show

questions.explanation: A survey measures intention at one moment, not the final vote. With 23% undecided and a five point gap, the margin depends on how late movement resolves, so this is a lean rather than a winner.
questions.hint: Weigh the size of the gap against the undecided share.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Locate where a threshold rule blocks a small party from winning seats.
questions.stem: A diagram I sketched in my logbook sets out the association's rule: votes are pooled by party, a party below five per cent is set aside, and the remaining parties share the seats in proportion to their totals.

options.text: At the pooling stage, because votes from small parties are merged with the large ones
options.misconception: misplaces the threshold at a stage that follows the exclusion

options.text: At the seating stage, because only parties clearing five per cent can take a seat
options.misconception: repeats the threshold instead of locating where it applies

options.text: At the nomination stage, because new parties struggle to find candidates willing to stand
options.misconception: confuses finding candidates with how seats are allocated

options.text: At the exclusion step, because a party below the threshold is removed from the count

questions.explanation: The threshold is what stops new parties from winning seats: a party below the floor is dropped before the proportional division, so its support never reappears. That is why small parties must pool support before an election.
questions.hint: Ask where the five per cent rule actually operates.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how incumbency advantages accumulate across successive elections.
questions.stem: In my notebook I explain why the branch's sitting treasurer won her third consecutive election despite fewer members speaking in her support than for her opponent.

answer.exemplar: The treasurer benefits from things the challenger cannot buy: name recognition built up over years, a record that members can point to when they are asked, and control of the association's mailing list and meeting calendar. An incumbent can sit on the mailing list without a campaign, while a challenger must spend money and effort to reach the same members. None of this is improper and none of it breaks the rules, but together these advantages mean the contest is not decided on the merits of the two candidates. The remedy is not disqualification but a rotation of the offices that carry the strongest incumbency advantages, so that the benefit of holding office cannot be accumulated indefinitely.

questions.explanation: Incumbency advantages accumulate: recognition, records and control of the association's own communications. A challenger must spend effort to obtain what the incumbent already holds.
questions.hint: Ask what the challenger must buy that the incumbent has.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Count the seats of a tribunal that lie beyond the appointive body's control.
questions.stem: The association's review panel has nine seats: the committee appoints three, the assembly appoints four, and the panel elects two from among its own sitting members. How many seats sit outside the committee's control?
questions.explanation: Only the three committee appointments are controlled by the committee, so the other six seats are beyond its reach. Those six are what allow the panel to decide cases independently.
questions.hint: Subtract the controlled seats from the total.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Weigh the evidential value of a canvass report on a count in progress.

stimulus.body: Extract from the Fenwick branch canvass report, 5 May: The party's observers were given access to the count from the opening of the boxes and recorded the running total in each of the six polling districts. Their note states that the amber candidate led in four districts and the blue candidate led in two, and that no district changed its lead during the count.

questions.stem: According to the canvass report, what is the strongest support it provides?

options.text: The direction of the result is well evidenced, because no district changed its lead
The amber candidate won, since amber led in more districts than blue
options.misconception: counts districts as though each were weighted by its votes

options.text: The count was fair, since the observers were given access from the opening
options.misconception: conflates observer access with proof of a fair count

options.text: The margin was narrow, since two districts were led by the blue candidate
options.misconception: infers a margin from the number of districts won

questions.explanation: Observers watching every district from the opening and seeing no change of lead have good grounds on the direction of the result. They cannot supply the margin, because districts are not of equal size.
questions.hint: Ask what the observers could establish and what they could not.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the matter a transition agreement leaves unresolved.

stimulus.body: Extract from my logbook, summarising the Ashcombe transition agreement: The outgoing treasurer will complete the audit of the previous year before standing down, will publish the accounts of the previous three years in the spring bulletin, and will hand the cash box to the incoming treasurer on the day of the handover meeting. The agreement contains no provision for the rules of the next election.

questions.stem: Given the summary of the transition agreement, which matter does it leave unresolved?

options.text: The completion of the audit of the previous year's accounts
options.misconception: leaves out a duty the agreement clearly states

options.text: The publication of three years of accounts in the spring bulletin
options.misconception: leaves out an obligation the agreement clearly states

options.text: The rules under which the incoming treasurer and committee are chosen
The handover of the cash box on the day of the meeting
options.misconception: leaves out a term the agreement clearly states

questions.explanation: The agreement settles the audit, the accounts and the handover of the cash box, and says in terms that it contains no election provision. The rules for choosing the new committee therefore remain open.
questions.hint: Look for what the summary says the agreement does not contain.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compare two parties' seat and vote shares to identify a departure.
questions.stem: Comparing two counts in my logbook: the amber party took 28% of the vote and 41% of the seats, while the green party took 33% of the vote and 26% of the seats. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: Neither party is over-represented, because both seat shares lie near their vote shares
options.misconception: treats a small departure as though it were no departure at all

options.text: Seat gains and losses run in opposite directions, so the rule did not track votes
The result was proportional, because the two parties together hold a majority of seats
options.misconception: judges proportionality by the overall majority rather than each share

options.text: The green party was favoured, because its vote share exceeded its seat share
options.misconception: calls a party under-represented one that is over-represented

questions.explanation: Amber's seats exceed its votes by thirteen points while green's fall short by seven, so the allocation moved in both directions at once. The pattern is not proportional, though the cause needs more evidence.
questions.hint: Set each party's seat share beside its own vote share.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Apply a counting rule to an observation that arrived after closing.
questions.stem: First, the association's rules say a count closes when every ballot box has been opened and recorded. Second, one hill district's box was still sealed when the result was announced. What follows?

options.text: The count was invalid, because the rule requires every box to be opened before closing
options.misconception: assumes a rule that would void the whole count entirely

options.text: The result stands, because a sealed box cannot change the totals already counted
options.misconception: assumes the missing box cannot affect the margin

options.text: The candidates must be notified, but the count may still be declared on the boxes opened
options.misconception: invents a notification requirement the rules do not mention

options.text: The announced count did not satisfy the rule, because a box remained unopened

questions.explanation: Opening every box is a condition of closing the count, so with one box still sealed the condition was unmet. The announced total therefore rests on an incomplete set, whatever the size of the shortfall.
questions.hint: Check the condition the rule attaches to closing the count.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a change between two surveys reveals about opinion.
questions.stem: Over the autumn I recorded in my logbook that two surveys of the same branch gave the amber party leads of nine points and of two points in successive months.

options.text: The later survey is better, because earlier figures described an electorate that has since moved
options.misconception: dismisses the earlier reading without asking what changed

options.text: Neither figure is usable, because a survey never sees the same electorate twice
options.misconception: claims every survey sees a different electorate from the last

options.text: The change shows opinion moved toward amber, so both readings describe a moving electorate
The change shows the first survey was wrong, because its gap was much larger
options.misconception: infers an error from an ordinary change in measured opinion

questions.explanation: A nine point lead narrowing to two over one month shows that measured opinion was moving, which is what a live survey is expected to show. It does not show that either survey was conducted badly.
questions.hint: Ask what the two figures together show about change.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the effect of a threshold on a party that falls below it.
questions.stem: My logbook entry for the harvest meeting notes that the green party took 4.2% of the vote, below the 5% threshold, and won no seats.

options.text: The threshold kept the green party out of seat allocation despite its vote share
The green party lost the seats because the branch counts ballots with an error
options.misconception: invents a counting error the logbook never records

options.text: The green party would have won seats if the threshold had been set at three per cent
options.misconception: speculates about a rule the entry never discusses

options.text: The result was proportional, because the party received no seats and no more
options.misconception: confuses receiving nothing with receiving exactly what was owed

questions.explanation: The green party fell below the threshold, so it was excluded before seats were allocated. That is the ordinary effect of a threshold, which is why small parties complain that votes can be cast and then disregarded.
questions.hint: Ask whether the party was inside the threshold at all.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a narrowing margin of victory without over-reading it.
questions.stem: The figures in my logbook show that in the last two branch elections the sitting treasurer won by 310 votes and by 190 votes, against a challenger who had also narrowed a previous gap.

options.text: The shrinking margin shows the challenger's campaign became steadily more effective
options.misconception: credits the challenger with a change that favours the incumbent

options.text: The shrinking margin is consistent with incumbents winning more narrowly over time
The shrinking margin shows the association's membership is falling each year
options.misconception: invents a membership trend the figures do not record

options.text: The shrinking margin shows nothing, because two results cannot establish a pattern
options.misconception: insists on a larger sample than the question requires

questions.explanation: Two results cannot establish a trend, but they are consistent with an incumbent holding on more narrowly as opposition improves. The narrowing is at least as consistent with a stronger challenger.
questions.hint: Ask what else could produce a narrowing margin.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Trace how the composition of a tribunal protects its independence.
questions.stem: A flow chart in my logbook runs: the committee appoints three judges, the assembly appoints two, the panel elects two of its own members, and the panel hears disputes against the committee.

options.text: The committee can sway the panel, because nine judges are easy for one body to influence
options.misconception: asserts influence without counting the seats that are out of reach

options.text: The committee's three appointments are decisive, because the panel sits in odd numbers
options.misconception: assumes odd numbers alone determine who carries a decision

options.text: The structure is complete, because no further safeguard against pressure is needed
options.misconception: assumes adequacy where the question is the arithmetic of the seats

options.text: Six judges sit beyond the committee's control, which is the majority it would need

questions.explanation: Three of nine judges are committee appointments, so six sit outside its control and the majority cannot be stacked to the committee's liking. The seat arithmetic is what makes the structure protective.
questions.hint: Count the judges the committee does not appoint.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Set out what is required before a party-reported lead may be relied on.
questions.stem: In the logbook I keep beside the hives I explain what would be needed before the amber party's claimed lead of 900 votes could safely be reported.

answer.exemplar: A figure that comes from a party source and a party tally is a claim, not a finding, because the party has an interest in how it reads. Before it could be reported as the result it would have to be matched against the returning officer's official declaration for the same districts, and checked for the districts the party may have omitted or counted differently. The relevant test is whether the official count confirms both the direction and the rough size of the lead. If the two agree, the lead may be reported as the count; if they do not, the party figure must be dropped rather than softened, because an interested source is least reliable exactly where its claim is most striking.

questions.explanation: A party figure is an interested claim until it is checked against the returning officer's declaration. Reporting it as fact would lend it a confidence its source does not carry.
questions.hint: Ask what the official declaration says for those districts.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Count the handover items a transition agreement leaves outside finance.
questions.stem: The tally in my logbook for the transition agreement lists nine handover items, of which four are financial records. How many of the listed items are not financial records?
questions.explanation: Nine listed items less the four financial records leaves five items that are not financial, such as the hives, the extractor and the membership records. The handover covers the whole of the work.
questions.hint: Subtract the financial items from the total listed.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish what a record establishes about a result from what it leaves open.

stimulus.body: Extract from my notes on the March branch election: The green party polled 6.1 per cent of the vote across the branch as a whole but won no seats. The branch uses an eleven-member committee and the largest party takes six seats. No other party polled below 6 per cent.

questions.stem: According to my notes, which reading of the March result is best supported?

options.text: The green party's votes did not convert into seats, and the notes do not say why
The green party was excluded by the threshold, since its share was below ten per cent
options.misconception: invents a threshold figure the notes never state

options.text: The green party lost seats it had won before, so it must have held more last year
options.misconception: infers a previous result that the notes do not record

options.text: The result was proportional, because no party won more seats than its vote share
options.misconception: treats a single party's seat loss as proof of proportionality

questions.explanation: A party can poll six per cent and win nothing when seats go to the largest party alone. The notes do not say whether a threshold excluded it or its votes were spread thinly.
questions.hint: Ask what the notes do and do not record.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Read a late observation against the counting time fixed in advance.

stimulus.body: Note I wrote after the February count: The hill district's ballot box was opened at 9.10 p.m., which was after the hour announced in the notice. The chairman read the closing time aloud twice before counting began. The notice had been posted at the hall a fortnight earlier.

questions.stem: Given the note I wrote after the February count, how should the late box be treated?

options.text: As acceptable, because the chairman announced the actual closing time twice
options.misconception: reads a late announcement as prior authorisation

options.text: As a late observation outside the count the notice had set, which raises a question
As fatal to the whole election, because one late box voids every count in the branch
options.misconception: treats a local irregularity as voiding the whole election

options.text: As irrelevant, because the notice's hour was only a guide for members to attend
options.misconception: reinterprets a stated deadline as a loose suggestion

questions.explanation: The notice fixed an hour and the box arrived after it, with the actual time being announced rather than authorised. Whether the late observation counts is therefore open on the face of the note.
questions.hint: Ask whether the closing time was set or merely announced.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Choose the survey figure that best predicts an election outcome.
questions.stem: Working through the winter logbook, I ask which survey figure best predicts a result: one taken four months before the vote, one taken two weeks before, or the average of the two.

options.text: The earlier survey, because it reflects settled opinion before campaign effects began
options.misconception: ignores that campaigns shift opinion before the vote

options.text: The average of the two, because averaging two estimates is always more accurate
options.misconception: presumes that averaging cancels whatever error each survey had

options.text: The survey taken nearest the vote, because late opinions are the ones that turn out
Neither survey predicts anything, because surveys record opinions rather than decisions
options.misconception: dismisses the predictive value of intention measures entirely

questions.explanation: Intentions change most as the election approaches, and the final weeks are when undecided voters settle. The nearer survey tells more about how the vote will fall, though none removes error.
questions.hint: Ask which survey speaks for the electorate closest to the vote.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a threshold for entry to a ballot from the vote that wins a seat.
questions.stem: First, the association uses a single-member system with a five per cent threshold per district. Second, a new party has 5.2% in each of four districts and is second in one of them. What follows?

options.text: The party wins the seat, because 5.2% clears the threshold in every district
options.misconception: treats clearing the threshold as if it delivered the seat

options.text: The party wins the seat, because being second in a district is enough to take it
options.misconception: confuses entry requirements with the vote that wins a seat

options.text: The party is excluded everywhere, because a national share governs each district
options.misconception: applies a national threshold to separate district contests

options.text: The party is on the ballot in each district, but seats still turn on the district vote

questions.explanation: A threshold governs entry to the ballot, not who wins the seat. Clearing 5.2% puts the party on every ballot, but it takes the seat in a district only if the local vote puts it ahead.
questions.hint: Ask what the threshold decides and what it does not.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain incumbency advantage as a structural feature of the contest.
questions.stem: My logbook records that in the past three branch elections the winner had held office before, and the record also notes that each of those winners had personally delivered the branch's training sessions.

options.text: Incumbents convert visibility and standing into votes that challengers must buy
Incumbents win because challengers always make worse speeches than their rivals
options.misconception: substitutes speaking quality for a structural advantage

options.text: Incumbents win because voters prefer continuity and dislike any change at all
options.misconception: assumes a uniform voter preference that the record does not show

options.text: Incumbents win because the branch always runs more candidates than it can seat
options.misconception: invents a candidate shortage the logbook never mentions

questions.explanation: Visibility and standing are resources the incumbent holds before the contest begins, and they convert into votes a challenger must spend money and time to buy. That is a structural advantage of office.
questions.hint: Ask what the challenger must purchase before the vote.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why shared appointment and funding weaken a tribunal's independence.
questions.stem: The entry for the September meeting in my logbook records that the association's review panel hears disputes, that the committee appoints three of its nine judges, and that panel decisions are final.

options.text: The arrangement is sound, because panel decisions are final and cannot be revisited
options.misconception: treats finality as if it were a substitute for independence

options.text: The arrangement is sound, because panel members serve for a fixed nine-year term
options.misconception: relies on a term of office the logbook never mentions

options.text: The arrangement is exposed, because a third of the panel is appointed by one litigant
The arrangement is exposed, because finality prevents any further appeal at all
options.misconception: confuses the absence of appeal with the presence of pressure

questions.explanation: Independence is most secure when the body funding and appointing a tribunal is separate from it. Here the committee funds the panel and appoints a third of it, so it can shape outcomes without any order.
questions.hint: Ask whether one body both funds and appoints the panel.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compare a reported lead with an official margin across two districts.
questions.stem: I compared two results in my logbook: in one the reported lead was 900 votes and the official margin 860, in the other the reported lead was 1,200 and the official margin 110.

options.text: Both reports were accurate, since the two counties count in different ways
options.misconception: invents a counting difference to excuse two different errors

options.text: The Fenwick report overstated the lead, and the Marlow report was close
Neither report can be assessed, since official margins are themselves uncertain
options.misconception: declines the comparison without examining the figures at all

options.text: The figures agree, since both reports show a clear lead for the same party
options.misconception: treats two leads of different size as if they agreed

questions.explanation: Marlow's reported lead of 900 against an official 860 differs by forty votes, while Fenwick's reported 1,200 against an official 110 differs by over a thousand. One is close; the other inflated.
questions.hint: Subtract each official margin from the reported lead.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify what each term of a handover arrangement actually determines.
questions.stem: The sketch I drew in my logbook runs: outgoing officers hand over hives, extractor and cash box; records are preserved; the old president keeps the badge for the year; lawfulness disputes go to the county tribunal.

options.text: The third step fixes a personal entitlement and the fourth fixes a forum, not an outcome
The fourth step settles the lawfulness question outright, because the tribunal is neutral
options.misconception: confuses choosing where a dispute is heard with deciding it

options.text: The first step covers only property, since hives and extractors are not association assets
options.misconception: invents a distinction between private and association property

options.text: The second step expires with the old committee's term, so records need no preservation
options.misconception: reads a preservation duty as if it were a temporary one

questions.explanation: Keeping the badge for the year settles what a person may retain, while sending disputes to the county tribunal settles only where the argument is heard. The lawfulness question is still to be argued there.
questions.hint: Ask whether each term fixes an outcome or a procedure.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a paired set of seat and vote shares establishes and leaves open.
questions.stem: In the logbook I set out why a result in which the amber party won 40% of the vote and 30% of the seats while green won 35% of the vote and 42% of the seats deserves careful handling.

answer.exemplar: The two results are mirror images, and that is what makes them worth analysing: amber is short by ten points of seats against its votes while green is long by seven. A gap of that kind can arise from the allocation rule itself, from differences in how votes were spread between districts, or from an unequal distribution of seats between districts, and these figures alone cannot say which. What they do show is that representation did not follow votes, and that the departure ran in green's direction. Establishing the departure and explaining its cause are separate steps, and the second requires knowing which system was used and how its districts were drawn.

questions.explanation: The pair shows representation departing from votes in green's favour. Explaining whether the cause was the rule, the districts or the seat pattern needs information the log does not hold.
questions.hint: Ask what a departure from votes proves, and what it does not.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compute the total a count would reach if a late observation were included.
questions.stem: My count for the branch records that 1,463 valid ballots had been counted when the hill apiary's box arrived a week late with 37 more. How many valid ballots would the total have been if the late box had been counted?
questions.explanation: Adding the 37 ballots in the late box to the 1,463 already counted gives 1,500 valid ballots. The late observation would have raised the total by that amount, which may matter where the margin was small.
questions.hint: Add the late ballots to the count already made.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Weigh the coverage of a survey sample against the figures it produces.

stimulus.body: Extract from the committee minutes I copied into my logbook, 3 April: Of those who replied, 47 per cent said they would definitely or probably vote amber, 41 per cent said the same of blue, and 12 per cent said they had not yet decided. The editor's note records that the booklet was sent to 2,000 members and that 640 were returned.

questions.stem: According to the minutes, what should the reader keep in mind about these figures?

They describe the membership, because every member was given the chance to reply

options.text: They show a clear leader, because six points is a decisive gap between the parties
options.misconception: ignores the undecided share and the very low response rate

options.text: They show nothing at all, because a survey can never be used to plan a campaign
options.misconception: dismisses surveys as useless for any planning purpose

questions.explanation: The percentages are calculated on those who replied, and only 640 of 2,000 recipients did so. The figures describe a third of the membership at most, and a six point gap must be read against that.

options.misconception: changes the electorate without changing the contest itself

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate what a survey-to-result comparison does and does not establish.
questions.stem: In the notebook kept by the hives I compare a survey taken a month before the election, giving amber 44% and blue 42%, with the actual result of amber 41% and blue 44%. Explain what this comparison shows and what it does not.

answer.exemplar: The comparison shows that the survey pointed to the winner but not to the margin: amber led in the survey and won, yet by three points fewer than the survey implied, and blue trailed and then won. That is a familiar pattern, because undecided voters tend to break towards whichever candidate has a plausible route to victory rather than to the party they name first when pressed. What the comparison does not show is that the survey was wrong, since a survey is one estimate with its own margin of error, and a single election cannot separate that margin from a real tendency in the electorate to move in a particular direction. The comparison is evidence of a tendency across cases, not proof of a rule.

questions.explanation: The survey named the winner but not the margin, which fits the pattern of undecideds breaking towards a plausible winner. One comparison shows a pattern rather than a law.
questions.hint: Ask what the survey got right and what it got wrong.

questions.learningObjective: Trace how redistribution of excluded votes affects the final seat totals.

options.misconception: misses the later redistribution of the excluded votes

options.misconception: treats the measurement as the point of exclusion

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a large margin won without campaigning reveals about incumbency.
questions.stem: In the logbook by the hives I explain why the treasurer's third consecutive term was won by the largest margin in the branch's history even though she ran no campaign at all.

answer.exemplar: Winning without campaigning is itself the strongest evidence of incumbency, because a candidate who can win without advertising is drawing on something already held rather than on anything the contest produced. Three consecutive terms supply name recognition, a record that voters can point to, and standing with the officers who run the meeting, none of which has to be earned at election time. The large margin therefore reflects the depth of that standing rather than the strength of any platform, and it shows why equal campaign rules do not by themselves produce a fair contest. It also warns against reading the margin as evidence of satisfaction, since a treasurer's visibility may be a product of the office rather than a verdict on it.

questions.explanation: Winning without a campaign points to advantages already held, such as recognition and a record, rather than to persuasion. Equal campaign rules do not by themselves produce an equal contest.
questions.hint: Ask what the absence of a campaign reveals.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why a national vote share can fail to produce seats in any district.

options.misconception: applies a national share to a district-by-district contest

options.text: Both outcomes show the threshold did not operate, since no party was excluded at all
options.misconception: assumes no party was excluded without supporting figures

options.text: The outcome turned on where the votes fell, since seats were won district by district
The result was proportional, since green's share of votes matched its share of seats
options.misconception: confuses an absent seat with a proportional result

questions.explanation: A party above five per cent nationally can fail in every district if its support is spread thinly, as green's was across eleven districts. The result reflects the geography of the vote, not the threshold.
questions.hint: Ask where the party's votes actually fell.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Attribute a narrowing margin to the most plausible cause the record allows.
questions.stem: I compared two tallies in my logbook: in the first the incumbent faced a first-time challenger and won by 400 votes; in the second the same treasurer faced a challenger who had polled 30% the year before and won by 60.

options.text: The incumbent's advantage fell by 340 votes, which suggests challengers grow stronger each year
options.misconception: reads a margin change as a general trend among challengers

options.text: The margin narrowed by 340 votes, which is consistent with a stronger challenger rather than a weaker incumbent
The two results show no pattern, since 400 and 60 are both ordinary winning margins
options.misconception: treats a large change in margin as unremarkable

options.text: The incumbent's advantage grew, since a smaller winning margin means a stronger incumbent
options.misconception: reads a narrower margin as a stronger incumbent

questions.explanation: The margin fell from 400 to 60, a narrowing of 340, while the only recorded change is the challenger's identity. That is consistent with a more experienced opponent eroding the incumbent's advantage.
questions.hint: Compare the two margins and note what else changed.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Locate the stage in a decision route where improper influence could go unseen.
questions.stem: A diagram in my notebook runs: a claim is filed, judges are assigned from the panel, evidence is heard, judgment is given, the judgment is published, and a member may apply to the county tribunal for review.

options.text: At the assignment stage, since the committee appoints three of the nine judges
options.misconception: identifies a stage the diagram shows as free of control

options.text: At the publication stage, since the reasons are what a later challenge must attack
options.misconception: treats transparency as the weak point in the route

options.text: At the review stage, since no appeal may lie from the county tribunal
options.misconception: invents a restriction the diagram does not record

options.text: At the judgment stage, where a ruling in the committee's favour is reached in private

questions.explanation: The route shows no stage at which committee influence could be seen, and judgment comes before reasons and review. The one point where improper influence could enter unseen is the hearing of evidence.
questions.hint: Ask at which stage nobody is watching.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a partial unofficial tally does and does not establish.
questions.stem: In the notebook by the hives I set out what a single observer's sighting of handwritten tallies on a hall board does and does not establish about the result.

answer.exemplar: A hand-written figure on a hall board is an intermediate record, not the count itself, and its reliability depends on who wrote it and when. An observer who saw the board at ten o'clock knows what the board said at ten o'clock, which may predate later additions, corrections or the arrival of stations whose results were held back. That is enough to suggest a direction if the board was complete and kept honestly, and far too little to publish as a margin, because the number of stations behind it is unknown and the writer had no duty to the observer. A figure of this kind becomes usable only when it can be matched against the returning officer's declaration, which fixes both the total and the stations it covers. Until then it should be described as a partial count rather than as a lead.

questions.explanation: A board tally is a partial and unofficial record, good for a direction at best. It becomes a result only when it can be matched against the returning officer's declaration.
questions.hint: Ask how many stations the board tally covered.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compute the handover effort a transition agreement requires.
questions.stem: My count of the branch's meetings notes that the transition agreement requires the outgoing committee to settle the accounts of each of the six apiaries, taking three meetings per apiary. How many meetings does the handover require?
questions.explanation: Six apiaries at three meetings each is 18 meetings of handover work for the outgoing committee to fit in before it stands down. The figure shows how costly a thorough handover can be.
questions.hint: Multiply the number of apiaries by the meetings each needs.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain a seat pattern produced by district contests rather than national totals.

stimulus.body: Extract from the committee minutes I copied into my logbook, 8 June: The report of the returning officer records that the blue party received 4,120 votes, the amber party 4,050 and the green party 1,830, and that the seven seats were distributed as three to blue, two to amber, one to green and one to the candidate who came last overall. The minutes note that the branch uses a first-past-the-post system in each district.

questions.stem: According to the minutes, which reading of the seven-seat result is best supported?

options.text: The result was disproportionate, because green won a seat with far fewer votes than blue
options.misconception: compares aggregate votes with seats won in separate contests

options.text: The result was proportional, because each party won seats in proportion to its votes
options.misconception: ignores the first-past-the-post rule the minutes set out

options.text: The seat pattern follows the district contests, and the aggregate vote totals explain little
The result was disproportional, because the last candidate won a seat no rival exceeded
options.misconception: complains about the winner without noting how the system works

questions.explanation: Under a first-past-the-post system, seats follow the result in each district, not the national totals, so a party with fewer votes overall can win more seats. The aggregate figures explain little.
questions.hint: Ask whether seats follow national totals or districts.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Classify a result announced before all polling stations reported.

stimulus.body: Note from my logbook, 4 April: The count for the Fenwick branch was closed at 9 p.m. with nineteen of the twenty-one polling stations reported. The hill farms had not reported because the carrier had broken down on the road. The branch secretary wrote in the margin of the page that the count would be reconvened once the two stations reported.

questions.stem: Given the note, what is the status of the result announced on the night of 4 April?

options.text: Provisional only, since two stations were missing and the secretary expected to reconvene
Final, since the branch secretary's signature settles the count
options.misconception: treats a signature as proof the count was complete

options.text: Void, because the count should not have been closed without every station
options.misconception: prescribes total invalidity where the note expects reconvening

options.text: Unchanged, because two stations out of twenty-one could not alter the outcome
options.misconception: assumes a missing station could never change a close result

questions.explanation: Two of twenty-one stations had not reported, and the note records that the count would be reconvened once they did. The result announced that night was provisional, not the final count.
questions.hint: Ask what the secretary expected to happen next.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Choose the survey reform that addresses the main weakness of the sample.
questions.stem: In my logbook I weigh which change to the branch's survey would most improve its usefulness for predicting next year's result.

options.text: Publish more of the individual replies, so that patterns within the sample can be inspected
options.misconception: adds transparency without improving the sample's coverage

options.text: Ask every member, and use weighting to correct for those who reply least often
Ask fewer, more detailed questions, so the survey costs less to run each year
options.misconception: reduces cost while leaving the sample's bias untouched

options.text: Ask the same question each year, so the results can be compared over time
options.misconception: values comparability over the accuracy of any single wave

questions.explanation: The weakness is coverage: only those who reply are measured, and they may differ from the membership. Asking everyone and weighting by reply patterns corrects for that; the other changes do not.
questions.hint: Ask which weakness in the survey the change would remove.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Assess one party's proportionality under a rule with a threshold.
questions.stem: First, the branch's rule allocates seats strictly in proportion to vote shares with a five per cent threshold. Second, amber took 30% of the vote and 30% of the seats. What follows?

options.text: The result was still disproportional, because the threshold excluded the green party
options.misconception: judges one party's result by another party's exclusion

options.text: The result was disproportional, because amber should have won more seats than it did
options.misconception: assumes a rule that rewards a party beyond its vote share

options.text: The result cannot be assessed, because a threshold always creates some disproportion
options.misconception: declines the assessment the figures actually permit

options.text: Amber's outcome was proportional, since its seat share matched its vote share exactly

questions.explanation: A threshold can create departures for small parties, but amber's seat share equals its vote share, so its outcome shows no deviation. The threshold bears on parties below the floor, not on amber.
questions.hint: Compare amber's two percentages directly.
